o: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, and altered consciousness

High TSH level accompanied by completely normal T4 level
qs.e: Myxedema coma = decompensated severe hypothyroidism. Precipitated by cold, infection, or sedatives in elderly. Features: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, altered consciousness. Treatment: IV T3/T4 + hydrocortisone + supportive care.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Coma is a profound, sustained loss of consciousness with no purposeful response, requiring urgent evaluation of reversible causes and supportive care. It is staged by the Glasgow Coma Scale and classified by underlying pathology. Rapid, systematic assessment saves lives.

sections.p: Coma is defined as a state of unconsciousness lasting longer than 30 minutes, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8 or less, and no purposeful response to stimuli. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by history, examination and basic investigations.
The Glasgow Coma Scale stages coma into mild (GCS 9–12), moderate (GCS 5–8), and severe (GCS 3–4). Severity correlates with prognosis and guides urgency of intervention.
b: Severe: GCS 3–4, imminent risk of death

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top causes are infections (malaria, meningitis, HIV encephalopathy), metabolic disturbances (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia), toxins (herbal, alcohol), and trauma. Treat the most common first.
Patients are unresponsive, with no purposeful movement. Eye opening is absent or minimal. Breathing may be irregular, and pupils are often dilated and fixed.
b: Pupils may be equal, dilated, or anisocoric

sections.p: Investigations aim to identify reversible causes and guide management. Prioritise tests that are available locally and interpret results in context.

t.b: Normal CT does not rule out infection or metabolic causes

sections.p: Red flags include sudden onset, focal neurological signs, seizures, or signs of increased intracranial pressure. Complications are hypoxia, aspiration, pressure sores, and secondary infections.
Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care: airway protection, oxygen, glucose correction, and seizure control. Use drugs with proven efficacy and minimal toxicity.
b: Fluid balance: isotonic crystalloids, avoid overload

sections.p: After stabilization, monitor neurological status, repeat imaging if indicated, and treat underlying disease. Prevention focuses on vaccination, malaria prophylaxis, and safe medication use.
b: Use insecticide‑treated nets to prevent malaria

sections.p: Unconsciousness can be mistaken for sleep, intoxication, or delirium. Distinguish by lack of response to pain and absence of protective reflexes.
b: Delirium: fluctuating consciousness, but patient can follow simple commands

sections.p: Normal glucose or electrolytes do not exclude metabolic encephalopathy if sampling is delayed. A normal CT may miss early haemorrhage or infection.
b: Normal electrolytes can be seen in early hyponatraemia if not repeated

whenToSeekHelp: Breathing difficulty or abnormal breathing pattern

faq.q: What is the quickest way to assess coma severity?
faq.a: Use the Glasgow Coma Scale; a score of 8 or less confirms coma.

faq.q: Can a normal CT rule out a brain tumour?
faq.a: No; early tumours may not be visible, and normal CT does not exclude infection or metabolic causes.

faq.q: Is hypoglycaemia the most common reversible cause?
faq.a: Yes; it is rapidly correctable and should be checked immediately in any unconscious patient.
